analysis.one_liner: Sets deadlines and binding arbitration to speed up first union contracts.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 230-193 on June 9, 2026, with 210 of 212 voting Democrats in favor and 20 Republicans; the Senate has not voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers vote to form a union, getting the first contract signed often takes a year or more — an average of 465 days in one 2021 study — and employers can use that delay to wear down support for the union. This bill puts the process on a clock: bargaining must start within 10 days of the union being recognized, mediation by a federal service kicks in after 90 days without a deal, and if mediation fails within 30 days, a three-person arbitration panel — one member chosen by each side plus a neutral — decides the contract terms, binding for two years. It also bars employers from cutting wages or changing conditions while first-contract talks are underway, and requires a report on how long contracts actually take.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who have just voted to form a union and are waiting for their first contract — the group the bill's findings say waits an average of 465 days while employers drag out bargaining. The bill gives them a guaranteed bargaining start date, federal mediation after 90 days, and a binding arbitrator's decision if talks still fail, so they can begin collecting negotiated wages and benefits far sooner. Existing union members also gain from the rule barring employers from changing wages and conditions during first-contract talks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Newly unionized workers awaiting first contracts

how_it_helps.text: Employers must start bargaining within 10 days of a written request from a newly recognized union, ending the slow-walking that can drag out a first contract for a year or more.

If no deal is reached after 90 days, the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service must mediate; if mediation fails within 30 days, a three-person arbitration panel settles the dispute, and its decision is binding for two years.
While bargaining is underway, the employer must keep wages, hours, and working conditions unchanged, so workers' pay cannot be cut simply because they organized.
The arbitrators must weigh workers' cost of living, their ability to support their families, and comparable wages in the industry — not just the employer's finances.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that prefer to delay or avoid first contracts — they lose the ability to stall for a year or more, must keep pay and conditions unchanged during bargaining, and can have a two-year contract imposed by an arbitration panel. Employers in tight financial straits bear the greatest risk of arbitration terms they did not negotiate.

drawbacks.text: The bill substitutes a three-person arbitration panel's decision for a freely negotiated deal when talks break down, meaning a third party — not the workers or the employer — sets wages, benefits, and work rules for two years.

The binding contract lasts two years and can only be amended by written consent of both parties, so workers who later want to strike for better terms during that period are locked into the arbitrator's deal.

Employers — especially small businesses with tight finances — lose the flexibility of open-ended bargaining and can have contract costs imposed on them based on an arbitrator's weighing of their financial prospects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and measurable: the bill attacks a documented delay — an average of 465 days between a union winning an election and signing a first contract — by putting a 10-day start deadline, a 90-day mediation window, and a 30-day mediation clock on the process, with arbitration factors that include workers' cost of living and the employer's ability to pay [S2][S3]. The main cost is honest and serious: binding arbitration lets a three-person panel write the terms of a two-year contract instead of the workers and management negotiating freely, which many in the labor movement have historically resisted on principle, and it can impose contract costs on small employers with thin margins [S2][S3]. The bill also leaves no deadline on the arbitration panel itself. On balance, it shifts the process decisively toward workers who just won a union vote, at a real but bounded cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 230-193 and sent it to the Senate, where it has sat since June 10, 2026, without a vote; Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 16, 2025, and referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which did not act on it before the bill reached the floor.
On June 9, 2026, the House took it up under a rule and debated it for one hour.
The House passed it 230-193, with 210 of 212 voting Democrats in favor, 20 of 212 voting Republicans in favor, and the one Independent voting no.
The Senate received the bill on June 10, 2026; it has not been voted on, and the Congress is still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final outcome yet. If the bill stalls without a Senate vote, the winners are employers that resist unions, which keep the ability to delay first contracts until worker support erodes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Too early — employers hold the odds for now

sides.party_line_note: Democrats supported it nearly unanimously (210 of 212 voting yes) while 192 of the voting Republicans opposed it; 20 Republicans crossed over to pass it 230-193.

industries.note: The bill makes the union the guaranteed channel for a faster first contract by putting a clock and an arbitration backstop on bargaining — it entrenches unions' role in representing newly organized workers. Workers who just voted to unionize gain the most from that.

The bill removes the main tool such employers have for weakening new unions: dragging out first-contract talks until worker support fades. They must bargain on a clock, hold wages steady, and accept a binding arbitrator's deal if talks fail.
The agency gains a new mandatory role: every first-contract dispute unresolved after 90 days comes to it for mediation, and it runs the arbitration referral process.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats, and only 20 of 223 House Republicans supported it in the House. Bills that pass one chamber with overwhelmingly one-party support rarely get floor time in a Senate controlled by the other party, especially in the final two years of a Congress. The most likely path is that the bill waits out the session without a Senate vote and expires in January 2027, unless supporters attach it to a larger must-pass bill.
